title: Policies to alleviate poverty and redistribute income

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Set out the policies a government holds against poverty, from grants, progressive taxes and a minimum wage to promoting economic growth and improving education; trace how each works, and weigh strength against drawback.

blocks.heading: Policies that redistribute income directly
blocks.text: To redistribute income is to narrow the gap between the highest and lowest incomes, moving spending power from the better-off to the worse-off. The main direct policies: progressive taxation, which takes a larger share of income from high earners than from low earners; more generous transfer payments, such as the old-age pension, child grants and unemployment benefits, which put money straight into low-income households; a minimum wage, which sets a legal floor under pay; and direct provision, such as free basic schooling and state healthcare, which gives poor households services they could not buy. Brazil ties family grants to school attendance, and the Netherlands holds pensioner incomes up through transfers - the same levers outside southern Africa.

blocks.heading: A grant traced to the line
blocks.text: Trace a transfer. A household of four in Otavi earns N$2 400 a month, which is N$600 per person, below the absolute line of N$700. The government pays a child grant of N$250 per child a month, and the household has two children, so the grant adds 2 x N$250 = N$500. Household income becomes N$2 400 + N$500 = N$2 900, which is N$725 per person: the grant carries the household across the absolute poverty line. Because the grant is paid for each child in school, attendance tends to rise as well, which works on the weak skills that caused the low income in the first place.

blocks.heading: Strength, and the drawbacks that temper it
blocks.text: Grants work fast and reach households no employer can help - that is their strength. The drawbacks temper them. A poverty trap: as a household earns more, its grants are withdrawn, so the gain from extra work is small and some earners may decide work does not pay. Cost: transfers and free services must be funded from taxation, so a wide programme may strain the budget or force other spending down. The minimum wage has its own limit: where the floor is set above the market wage, firms take on fewer workers than want jobs at that pay - more so where demand for that labour is elastic - so the policy aimed at the poor may add to joblessness among them.

blocks.heading: Longer-run policies: promoting growth and improving education
blocks.text:
Grants and minimum wages act on today's incomes. Two further policies work on the causes, over years rather than months.

Promoting economic growth: when output grows, firms take on more workers and may pay more, so unemployed people find work and the low-paid gain hours. Growth also brings in more tax revenue at the same tax rates, which can fund pensions, grants, clinics and schools. Growth may therefore lift households out of poverty, provided the gains are shared with low-income households: where growth comes from a mine or an oil field that employs few people, or the new jobs need skills the poor do not have, poverty may fall little while average income rises. In China, rapid growth over several decades lifted hundreds of millions of people out of absolute poverty, while income gaps widened at the same time.

Improving education: schooling and training raise workers' skills and productivity, so they can get better-paid jobs and are less likely to be unemployed. Education also breaks the cycle in which poor parents cannot afford schooling for their children. A young person in Rundu who trains as an electrician may earn several times what casual labour pays. The drawbacks are time and cost: the benefit appears years later, the government must fund teachers and schools, and skills raise incomes only where there are jobs that use them.
